analysis.one_liner: Requires drug makers to sell prescriptions to seniors at the government's lowest negotiated price.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or floor vote in the Senate Finance Committee and died when the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required drug manufacturers that sell to the federal government to also sell their drugs to pharmacies serving Medicare beneficiaries at the lower of the lowest federal price or the manufacturer's 'best price' — the cheapest price it gives anyone [S2, S3]. Sponsors said this would cut seniors' prescription costs by more than 40 percent [S3]. The Senate referred it to the Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it; the bill died when the Congress ended [S1, S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who buy their own prescriptions out of pocket, since Medicare in 2001 did not cover outpatient drugs and seniors paid retail prices at the pharmacy. The bill's findings say they paid on average twice as much as the government and insurers paid for the same drugs, and sponsors estimated savings of more than 40 percent [S3]. Terminally ill hospice patients would also be covered [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill's findings state that older Americans who buy their own prescriptions pay, on average, twice as much as the drug makers' most favored customers such as health insurers and the federal government, and in some cases over 15 times more [S3].

It would require any drug manufacturer that sells to the United States government to make its drugs available to pharmacies serving Medicare beneficiaries at the lower of the lowest federal price or the manufacturer's best price [S3].

The sponsors estimated the change would reduce prescription drug prices for Medicare beneficiaries by more than 40 percent, and said more than 1 in 8 older Americans were forced to choose between food and medicine [S3].
It extended the same pricing to drugs furnished through Medicare-certified hospice programs, covering terminally ill patients [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would have to extend their lowest government or 'best price' to the pharmacy market for Medicare beneficiaries. The bill's own findings credit the current pricing gap with sustaining about $20 billion in annual industry profits [S3]. Taxpayers could also see lower Medicare costs as drug prices fell [S3].

drawbacks.text: Requiring manufacturers to sell drugs at their best price or the lowest federal price would cut into the industry's roughly $20 billion in annual profits, and the industry's standard objection is that lower expected revenue could reduce the money available for developing new drugs. The bill's own findings acknowledge the $20 billion profit figure it would draw from [S3].

The bill only helps Medicare beneficiaries; it would not lower drug prices for the roughly two-thirds of Americans under 65 who lack drug coverage, and it does not add a drug benefit to Medicare itself. It also relies on the Medicaid 'best price' formula, which manufacturers had a history of structuring rebate deals around, so the promised savings depended on enforcement the bill leaves to future regulations [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the seniors who pay cash at the pharmacy counter, the benefit is direct and large: a price floor tied to what the government already pays, with the bill's sponsors estimating savings above 40% [S3]. The cost falls on drug manufacturers, whose profits the bill's own findings put at $20 billion a year, and the main honest objection is that lower revenue could mean less investment in new drugs. A secondary gap: the bill helps only Medicare beneficiaries, leaving uninsured people under 65 out. On balance it is a targeted transfer from industry margins to older Americans' medicine budgets, and its main weakness is design reach rather than intent.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read the bill twice, sent it to the Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tim Johnson introduced S. 125 on January 22, 2001, and the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day [S1, S5].
The committee took no further action on the bill; the complete action history shows only the referral and three sets of sponsor introductory remarks over seven months [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or Senate floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers kept charging Medicare beneficiaries full retail prices, preserving the pricing gap the bill targeted, and the Finance Committee's members avoided a vote on the issue for the rest of the Congress.

for.name: Tim Johnson
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it three times during 2001.

for.name: 9 of 49 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Kennedy, Dorgan, Bingaman, Feingold, Leahy, Inouye, Kerry, Conrad).

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over Medicare
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 22, 2001 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the life of the Congress.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America
against.what_they_did: Fiercely opposed price-negotiation and 'best price' proposals during this period, arguing they were price controls that would reduce research investment.

sides.party_line_note: All ten Senate supporters were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; the bill never advanced past its party-of-origin committee referral [S4, S5].

industries.note: The bill would force any manufacturer selling to the federal government to offer its drugs to pharmacies serving Medicare beneficiaries at the lowest federal price or its Medicaid best price, whichever is lower [S3]. The bill's findings attribute about $20 billion a year in industry profits to the pricing gap that seniors currently pay [S3].

Pharmacies would gain access to cheaper wholesale stock for their Medicare customers, but would have to pass the lower prices on rather than keep the margin [S3]. The bill leaves their role intact and simply makes them the channel through which the discount reaches seniors.
